candidates.source_title: New bid for extra trains from Rochdale to London is refused - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans to improve the rail link between Rochdale and London have hit the buffers again. Today, the Office of Rail and Road announced it had rejected proposals for new train services which would have seen Lumo operate up to four additional return Rochdale-to-Euston services on weekdays and Saturdays and three services on Sundays . Among those backing calls for the extra services was Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, who called Lumo’s bid to restore six daily direct services between Rochdale and the capital a “game-changing opportunity” for the borough and the wider North West. But the ORR rejected the plans after its assessment found adding more trains to the West Coast Main Line — which also included services to Blackpool and Wrexham — would likely increase delays and cancelled trains for passengers. It said its assessment following detailed and extensive analysis is that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the West Coast Main Line has not materially changed since it rejected a similar application by Lumo last year. An external review commissioned by ORR also supported this conclusion. READ MORE: Police target crime gang’s ‘spider web of criminality’ The ORR said gaps in the current timetable need to provide important space for trains to recover when disruption occurs, minimising delays to passengers.

candidates.source_title: Win will help keep cottage cosy this winter - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A retired civil servant will be keeping extra warm this winter after winning 500 litres of heating oil. Liz Shrewsbury, who lives in a hamlet just outside Rochdale, won the prize in Craggs Energy’s Cosy Heating Club quarterly oil draw. Liz and her partner, Andrea, have lived in their 18th century cottage for 25 years. Liz said: “When Craggs Energy called me, I found myself thinking someone was playing a joke on me. It’s fair to say I was pretty much speechless! “I joined the Cosy Heating Club around two years ago, finding it a great way to spread the cost of our heating each month, instead of making bulk payments for each purchase. “It really helps with budgeting, even more so now the cost of oil has risen so much in the last 6 months. However, I’d completely missed that as a Direct Debit customer, I’d been automatically entered into the Cosy Heating Club quarterly prize draw. So, that was a great surprise! “Now that I know, I’ve been sharing that fact with all my neighbours that use heating oil, as the entire hamlet is off-grid. “I was due to order a tank refill, so the call came at the perfect time. The money saved will help balance out increased transport fuel prices and rising day-to-day living costs, all of which seem to have been escalating so much in the last year.”

candidates.source_title: Hopwood Hall ‘will be brought back into community use’
candidates.source_body_excerpt: After a turbulent two years of battling over Hopwood Hall, Rochdale’s council leader says the ‘cherished’ historic building will be brought back into use. Council bosses were quizzed over the future of the Middleton site following a High Court battle where the town hall prevailed against Hopwood DePree. The two day trial in Manchester Civil Justice Centre ruled that the council was not acting unlawfully when it ended an exclusivity agreement with the American filmmaker. Mr DePree entered an option agreement with the council to restore the hall back in 2017, until that agreement was ended in October 2024. Since then, Mr DePree, who claims ancestral connections with the 1400s stately home, has felt he had a legally binding agreement to purchase Hopwood Hall for £1. The High Court found that the ‘change of use’ planning approval was granted in 2022 wasn’t enough to trigger the option to purchase the hall for a ‘peppercorn fee’ – £1. In the first town hall meeting since the trial last month, council leader Neil Emmott was asked what the next steps were for the hall. Coun Emmott did not clarify a specific use for the future of the hall, but vowed to bring it back into use for the wider community. The council boss told the chamber on October 15 how his ‘door is always open’ to Hopwood DePree. Coun Emmott said if Mr DePree came back with a viable plan for the future of Hopwood Hall, the council would listen. In response to Coun Steve Potter’s question about the next steps for Hopwood Hall, Coun Emmott said: “The High Court’s judgment in relation to Hopwood Hall does not necessarily mark the end of the legal process. “Mr DePree has the right to seek permission to appeal the decision. The court has directed that any application for permission to appeal must be lodged by November 18, 2026, although there is scope for this deadline to be extended to November 28, 2026.
candidates.source_summary: After a turbulent two years of battling over Hopwood Hall, Rochdale’s council leader says the ‘cherished’ historic building will be brought back into use.

candidates.source_title: Town hall fears for the future of pubs
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Is the future of the local pub in danger? That’s the fear in Littleborough where the closure of another pub has sparked outcry. A few months ago The Wheatsheaf closed down in the Rochdalian town. There is strong community interest in reopening the pub as a local asset, but a small loophole means they fear they can’t do that. When breweries or large companies that own and operate pubs sell on the building, they can include a covenant that prevents it from being re-used as a pub. This covenant is inserted into a sale to stop competitors taking the pub on the cheap, the latest town hall meeting was told. Coun Richard Jackson brought forward a motion to Rochdale council to address this very issue to reduce the continued loss of pubs in communities. The Littleborough Lakeside councillor told the chamber on October 15: “The reality is that around 50 per cent of pubs are owned by breweries or large pub companies. They have a history of damaging the industry as a whole. This often leads to tenant attrition. “We are acutely aware of pubs being closed down after numerous tenants have left the building. The point of this motion is to address the churn. “We have seen this at the former Royal Oak pub. This was sold with an anti-competition covenant.” The former Royal Oak pub was closed down in 2015 and then sold off and became a vape shop, which was later shut down by Trading Standards.

candidates.source_title: Bonfire night events taking place in Rochdale
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Bonfire night is set to go off with a bang in Rochdale with a week full of events on offer. Yet again the council is putting on three firework display events in Rochdale, Heywood and Middleton – completely free of charge. Just like last year, Bowlee Community Park, Queens Park Road and Cronkeyshaw Common will all be dazzled by pyrotechnics. This year Rochdale council are trialling reduced noise firework displays to make the events more accessible to all. Festivities will begin on Monday, November 2 at Bowlee Community Park in Middleton. The next day (October 3) will be Heywood’s Queen’s Park Road event followed by the Cronkeyshaw Common event in Syke on October 4. All three of the council-run events will see the bonfire lit at 7pm and fireworks starting from 7.30pm. Food and soft drinks will be available to buy. Alcohol will not be on sale, nor is anyone allowed to bring their own alcohol, fireworks, or sparklers. There will be no toilet facilities provided at any of the three council-run events. Those planning to head to one of the organised displays have been urged by the council to walk or use public transport if possible due to limited parking availability. Elsewhere in the borough there are other options available to people. Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth are both putting on firework displays on Saturday, November 7.

candidates.source_title: Historic pub objects to plan for 17-storey tower nearby
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans for the 17-storey tower have prompted concerns over the Marble Arch's future A historic Manchester pub that has drawn visitors from around the world is fearing for its future amid plans for a large tower to be built nearby. The Marble Arch has been serving pints on Rochdale Road since 1888 when Queen Victoria sat on the throne and the city was rapidly industrialising. Plans by the McGoff Group to build a 17-storey tower with 153 flats next to the Grade II-listed pub have prompted concerns about the visual impact and the pub's continued existence. Manchester City Council said it accepted "some visual harm" would be caused as a result of the building going up, but would be "outweighed by the substantial public and regeneration benefits that the proposal would deliver". Councillors in Manchester have been recommended to approve the plans at a meeting on 22 October. The McGoff Group has been approached for a comment. Meanwhile, the Marble Arch has submitted a detailed objection against the plans, alongside the Victorian Society and Campaign for Real Ale.

candidates.source_title: Court rules in ownership row over Hopwood Hall - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A court has ruled that Rochdale Council did not act unfairly in its decision not to pass ownership of Hopwood Hall to one of its descendants. Today marked the end of a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester after Hopwood DePree took legal action against the council which ended an exclusivity agreement to sell the historic Grade II-listed hall to him. Following the decision, Mr DePree said: “This is of course incredibly disappointing and a huge blow to our community, our supporters around the world, as well as the UK’s charitable heritage rescue groups in general. “However, please know that my team and I are already determining our legal options and next steps. “We will be watching closely to keep an eye on Rochdale Borough Council’s efforts to save Hopwood Hall for the community, and restore it to its former glory.” Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. READ MORE:Rochdale Diversity Awards 2026 Finalists Announced

candidates.source_title: Town celebrates the people and stories behind Broadfield Park Slopes renovation - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The people who helped bring Rochdale’s historic Broadfield Park Slopes back to life were celebrated at a special event at Rochdale Town Hall. The celebration, arranged by Polly Brant, Rochdale Council Cultural Engagement officer, brought together volunteers, partners and people who have been involved in the project to recognise what has been achieved and, importantly, the contribution local people have made along the way. Guests watched a series of films created by Rochdale filmmaker Jack Grindrod and Breaking Barriers, capturing the people, stories, heritage and community involvement behind the transformation. The evening also featured poetry readings from Alende Amisi, a poet who grew up in Rochdale and was a young poet in residence during Rochdale’s Town of Culture. Passionate about the town and its heritage, Alende brought a personal perspective to an evening which was as much about Rochdale’s people as its history. A special thank you was also given to the many volunteers who have supported the project, giving their time to archaeological digs, activities and events and helping uncover and share the history of this important part of the town. The Grade II listed Broadfield Park Slopes sit between Rochdale Town Hall and St Chad’s Church and have been restored through a project delivered by Rochdale Development Agency working with Rochdale Borough Council, with funding from The National Lottery Heritage Fund. The work has restored the historic Packer Spout Fountain, created a new accessible pathway, improved landscaping, lighting and CCTV, and introduced new heritage interpretation. The lower lawn has also been terraced, creating a natural amphitheatre and new space for activities and events.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Find out the latest events from October 17 from All Across the Arts columnist Steve Cooke Directed by Anthony Almeida, this new production of Othello aims to take a fresh look at Shakespeare’s tragedy with a greater emphasis on class differences and love. Setting the play in the 1980s around soldiers at the time of the Falklands War is a bold move that achieves some of what the director intends. Watching the performance it is striking just how clearly the issue of race, rather than class, stands out. Othello is a very successful General and Desdemona’s father, Brabantio, clearly feels that Othello, although well suited for his role as an army General, is an unsuitable match for his daughter as he is a Moor. The staging, the army uniforms and attitudes of the soldiers are effective, but for some of us with memories from the 1980s they can be somewhat unsettling. The set is stark and dark with high chicken wire fences topped by barbed wire to represent the army compound which works well for this production. The arrival of Othello himself was a moment of high theatrical drama.

candidates.source_title: Leader outlines major investments, heritage rescue, and cost-of-living relief across Rochdale borough - InYourArea
candidates.source_body_excerpt: This week's column with Councillor Neil Emmott It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent Our Town, Our Future event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. It is an exciting time for the town, and we are turning ambition into action.

candidates.source_title: Two days that will decide the future of Hopwood Hall - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: The battle for Hopwood Hall returns to the courtroom today with ownership of the historic manor house at stake. Hopwood DePree and Rochdale Council begin a two-day trial in the High Court in Manchester later over Mr DePree’s bid to restore his ancestral home. Mr DePree is a descendant of the Hopwood family which build the manor house in the 1420s. The family owned the hall and surrounding land — which is now Hopwood Hall College — until 1922. The house was sold 20 years later. It was occupied by a variety of temporary residents, including the de la Salle Brothers, who ran it as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s. It had fallen into disrepair and was bought by Rochdale Council, which still owns the Grade II-listed property. The legal action initiated by Mr DePree was launched after he spent seven years working with the council to carry out vital repairs on the dilapidated site with a view to purchasing it. In November, 2024, the council ended its exclusivity agreement with Mr DePree, and said it would explore other options because no “commercially viable” business model had been presented. READ MORE: Four arrests and £1m drugs seizure in Rochdale Mr DePree’s case is that the council went back on his option to purchase Hopwood Hall upon planning permission being granted in 2022. His claim is that the agreement triggers have been satisfied and the council must proceed with the ownership transfer.

candidates.source_title: Hundreds object to plans to demolish house and build 45-home development - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans to demolish a house to pave the way for a new 45-home development are recommended for approval, despite more than 300 objections. Wain Homes has applied to Rochdale Council to demolish 58 Greenvale — Chadwick Farm Barn — in Bamford to create the access to the proposed development on land south of the property. The application will be determined by the council’s planning committee on Thursday due to the number of objections lodged against the proposals. Demolishing Chadwick Farm Barn would create access from Greenvale to the proposed development which includes 39 homes for market sale, split between 14 three-bed, seven four-bed and 18 five-bed, with six three and four-bedroom homes designated for social housing. A decision on the application was deferred in August due to a lack of a housing masterplan. Since then, the plans have received 311 additional responses, 304 of which objected to the development. They cite concerns regarding the premature release of the site ahead of a comprehensive housing masterplan, the inadequacy of local infrastructure, highway capacity and road safety, drainage and flooding, impacts on ecology and landscape and the effects upon the amenity of surrounding occupiers. candidates.source_title: No decision yet on College Bank – but ‘renovation would take more than a decade’ - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Renovating Rochdale’s iconic Seven Sisters tower blocks would force residents out of their homes for more than a decade, housing chiefs have said. While Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says no decision on the future of the landmark College Bank blocks has been taken, residents have asked new Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig to back their campaign to refurbish their homes rather than demolish them. But if campaigners get their wish, the scale of bringing the 61-year-old buildings up to modern standards would take more than 10 years and they could not be occupied until the work is complete, RBH chiefs have said. Members of Greater Manchester Tenants Union recently met Ms Craig to discuss the steps that could be taken to renovate almost 1,000 homes in College Bank and Lower Falinge. Plans to demolish College Bank were first discussed in 2017 when RBH warned that the buildings were approaching the end of their life. Tenants set up the Save the Seven Sisters campaign and hoped RBH’s partnership with Legal and General Affordable Homes would see the towers restored. But in September, 2024, it was announced that the partnership would not continue. The union and the Save the Seven Sisters campaign asked then Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham to help. In November, 2024, the Mayoral Taskforce was established to look at the options for the College Bank estate. Rochdale’s skyline without the Seven Sisters towers. Image: Copilot In October 2025, RBH announced the results of surveys which found the blocks were not safe to remain occupied and residents would be required to leave their homes.

candidates.source_title: Fate of major housing scheme on playing fields in Bamford to be decided
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Developers want to build 450 houses on former playing fields in Rochdale . The fate of one of the initial phases of the giant scheme will be decided next week. In August, Rochdale council ’s planning committee delayed making a decision on Wain Home’s plan to build 45 houses on a plot of land behind Greenvale, in Bamford. The committee felt they didn’t have enough detail about drainage from the developers. The site, to the west of Norden Road, has a history of flooding. So the panel of councillors wanted to ensure proper precautions were being taken by the developer before making a decision. Click here to get the biggest stories straight to your inbox in our Daily Newsletter This scheme would be the first of many for the former green belt land – which contains a number of playing fields and sports pitches. The Bamford site was taken out of green belt status after the adoption of the Greater Manchester housing strategy named Places for Everyone. A new clubhouse for Bridge FC and revamped sports pitches within the site are seen as the major benefits that would come from the overarching scheme. The plan would see access created through the demolition of Chadwick Farm Barn on Greenvale. In its place a T-junction would provide vehicle access to the site. It wasn’t just flood risks that the planning committee took issue with. Objectors at the meeting on August 5 raised concern over there being no safeguarding set in stone for how transport connectivity, drainage, highways, and local amenities would work across the whole site. To get the very latest from Manchester's political scene in your newsfeed - click here to add the MEN as your preferred Google source Planning agent Gareth Salthouse, representing Wain Homes, explained that drainage for the site had been assessed and said this plan could be done quickly to bring ‘much-needed housing’ to the area. The planning committee was also concerned about the lack of overall masterplan. Coun Tom Besford feared this ‘piecemeal development’ would see each developer do the bare minimum of affordable homes for each plot on the land. He felt this would eventually result in all the benefits not coming to fruition. Coun Besford said: “Why would we go through the blood, sweat and tears of getting PfE over the line but then just give this land away. We have to assume that we could get 10 other plans like this. “Then what if it doesn’t add up and everything falls short overall.” The committee agreed to defer the decision based on questions over drainage. candidates.source_title: Warning over scam callers impersonating police officers - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: People are being urged to remain vigilant following several reports of calls involving scammers impersonating police officers to obtain personal and sensitive information linked to cryptocurrency. Greater Manchester Police said one common method is to claim that they have arrested a suspect who was in possession of the victim’s personal documents, such as their passport, driving licence or banking details. On several occasions, fraudsters asked victims about their cryptocurrency accounts, specifically looking for their IDs, recovery phrases, and security codes. GMP says officers will never ask anyone to share this information or move your accounts. Police say the calls can appear convincing and are being made through spoofed GMP phone numbers. DS Reed, of GMP Cyber Crime Team, said: “These calls are an incredibly sophisticated type of crime, and those responsible are targeting our vulnerable communities. “We take offences of this nature incredibly seriously, and our team is working around the clock to understand how these offences have occurred, and how to prevent it from continuing. “Our officers will never get you to share security codes or personal information in relation to cryptocurrency, and if you are receiving calls that ask you to do so, please do not respond and report to us immediately.

candidates.source_title: Rochdale opens gateway to UK's next generation of advanced manufacturing - Industry News
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A major milestone has been reached for Atom Valley with completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale, which is set to become a nationally significant gateway driving the development of the advanced materials and manufacturing cluster in the region. The 30,000 sq. ft centre is the first major physical development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub for advanced materials and manufacturing in Rochdale, bringing together businesses, researchers, investors and innovation partners in one location. AVID provides an environment where organisations can innovate, grow and commercialise new technologies, strengthening Greater Manchester’s position as a leading centre for advanced materials and manufacturing. Completion of the building represents a major milestone for years of partnership working between Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), The University of Manchester and wider innovation partners. RDA has led the physical development of the SMMC, working with partners to secure investment and position advanced materials and manufacturing as a priority opportunity for Rochdale and Greater Manchester. The next phase will see work move from construction towards specialist fit-out ahead of bringing the centre into operation in 2027. The RDA brought together partners from industry, academia and government to establish the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023. Since then, businesses have been able to connect with a national network of specialist expertise, facilities and innovation support through the CEAMS partners, including The University of Manchester, the Henry Royce Institute, National Physical Laboratory (NPL), Centre for Process Innovation (CPI) and NCC (formerly National Composites Centre). CEAMS has already supported more than 90 companies, developing new products and processes and demonstrating the value of a more connected innovation ecosystem.

candidates.source_title: Borough means business as council delivers more pioneering projects - Rochdale Borough Council
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Left to right: Rose Marley and Steve Coogan, with Rochdale Borough Council Leader, Councillor Neil Emmott announcing new Middleton regeneration projects. It's been a busy and productive few weeks across our borough, with positive news, exciting regeneration projects and innovative services making a real difference for residents in Heywood, Middleton, the Pennines, and Rochdale. I want to begin with Hopwood Hall. The council welcomed the recent High Court judgement, which found in our favour and brings much-needed clarity about the future of this important historic building. While it's disappointing that a lengthy and potentially costly legal process was necessary, we are now focused on moving forward. Since 2017, more than £1.6 million has been invested in Hopwood Hall by the council and Historic England, and we remain committed to funding essential repairs. Feasibility studies have been completed and options for its long-term future will be considered in due course. What is certain is that, once restored, Hopwood Hall will serve the wider Middleton community and continue to play an important role in the town's rich heritage. There has also been a significant boost for Middleton's regeneration ambitions, with a series of announcements demonstrating the momentum building behind the town's Mayoral Development Corporation. I'm delighted that Middleton Old Grammar School, recently acquired by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. This follows news that the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be brought back into productive use, including the potential development of new homes. Meanwhile, plans are progressing to transform Middleton Scout Hut into a vibrant community venue offering activities and training opportunities for young people. There is more good news on the horizon, with banking and post office services set to return to Middleton town centre in the new year. This is something I have long championed and it will provide another welcome boost for the town centre. These projects form part of our wider commitment to invest in every part of the borough, creating jobs, driving economic growth and ensuring our communities thrive. At the recent 'Our Town, Our Future' event, I saw first-hand the passion local residents, businesses and community groups have for Middleton and their determination to shape its future. It is an exciting time for the town, and we are turning ambition into action. Supporting residents through the cost-of-living crisis also remains a key priority. I am proud of the help we have provided through our Helping Hand campaign, which has supported thousands of older and vulnerable residents since 2022. As global economic pressures continue to affect household finances, the council has recently approved a further package of support worth around £15 million over the next three years through the Government's Crisis and Resilience Fund. This will provide emergency financial assistance, help residents keep their homes warm, debt and welfare advice, housing support, access to food provision and free warm spaces.

candidates.source_title: Nominations open for Springhill Hospice’s 2026 Man of Rochdale award
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Springhill Hospice is inviting nominations for its 2026 Man of Rochdale award, recognising volunteers who help others across the borough. Nominations close at midnight on Monday 2 November. Nominees must live in the borough of Rochdale, be over 18 and give their time voluntarily for the benefit of the community. They must not have already received a Royal Award such as an MBE or OBE. The winner will be announced at an awards luncheon at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 27 November. The event starts at 1pm and includes a drinks reception, three-course lunch and guest speaker. Last year’s winner was Michael Bamford, who founded Re-Use Littleborough. The non-profit organisation helps families access essential items and supports children and communities overseas. John Shaw won in 2024 after receiving more than 40 nominations for his work supporting homeless and vulnerable people. He collects and distributes food, clothing and other essentials through the Good Solution Network and local charities. Springhill Hospice says this year’s ceremony will be its 32nd. The award is sponsored by Rochdale building and construction company Jackson Jackson and Sons. Victoria Barnett, senior corporate fundraiser at Springhill Hospice, said “This is our 32nd year running the event and each year seems to get better and better. That’s all thanks to the amazing community and local heroes who help to make the event so special and demonstrate the spirit of kindness, generosity, and compassion that defines the borough.” Tickets cost £65, with tables of ten available for £650. Proceeds will support the hospice’s care for adults with terminal or life-threatening illnesses and their loved ones across Rochdale.
